title: Palestinian Authority Delays Legislative Elections to 2025, Extending 20‑Year Voting Gap
body:
Ramallah – Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas on Friday issued a presidential decree that pushes the long‑awaited elections for the Palestinian Legislative Council back by another year, extending a hiatus that now stretches to two decades. The move means the next parliamentary vote, which was slated for 2024, will not take place until at least 2025, deepening concerns that the Palestinian political system is drifting further from democratic norms and widening the rift between the West Bank’s Fatah‑led administration and Hamas, which still controls Gaza.

The postponement follows a pattern that began in 2006, when Hamas won a sweeping victory over Fatah in the last legislative election. That result triggered a violent split between the two factions, leading Hamas to seize control of Gaza while the Palestinian Authority (PA) retained authority in the West Bank. Since then, multiple attempts to hold fresh elections have faltered amid disputes over voting locations, voter registration, and the status of East Jerusalem. Abbas, who has ruled the PA since 2005, cited “technical and logistical” challenges, as well as “the need to preserve national unity,” as justification for the additional delay.

Critics argue that the decree is less about practical obstacles and more about preserving Abbas’s grip on power. At 88, the president is constitutionally limited to two terms, yet he continues to serve without a fresh mandate, a situation that has drawn domestic and international criticism. The Palestinian Legislative Council, which has been largely dormant since 2007, remains a symbolic body with little legislative activity. By pushing the vote further into the future, Abbas effectively extends his de‑facto rule, while Hamas continues to claim legitimacy based on its 2006 victory.

The decision also reverberates beyond Palestinian politics, affecting the broader peace process. The United States, the European Union and several Arab states have repeatedly urged the Palestinians to hold elections as a confidence‑building measure that could revitalize stalled negotiations with Israel. Yet the internal deadlock hampers any meaningful dialogue, as Israel has signaled that a unified Palestinian leadership is a prerequisite for substantive talks. The postponement therefore risks further marginalizing the PA on the diplomatic stage and may embolden hard‑line elements on both sides of the conflict.

Human rights groups and civil society organizations within the territories have expressed disappointment, warning that repeated delays erode public trust in institutions. “Every year without a vote deepens the cynicism of ordinary Palestinians who already endure occupation, economic hardship and a lack of basic services,” said Leila Al‑Haddad, a spokesperson for the Palestinian Center for Democratic Development. “The legitimacy of the PA is already questioned; this decree only widens the democratic deficit.”

Looking ahead, the upcoming year will test whether the PA can overcome the logistical hurdles it cites and deliver a credible electoral process. International donors have indicated a willingness to fund the election if clear timelines are set, while Hamas has hinted it may participate if conditions allow for voting in East Jerusalem and Gaza. The window for reconciliation between Fatah and Hamas remains narrow, and the next election could either serve as a catalyst for unity or cement the status quo of division. As the calendar turns, the Palestinian public—and the world watching the conflict—will be waiting to see if the promised vote materializes or if postponement becomes the new norm.
